Longitudinal association between body weight change and brachial–ankle pulse wave velocity in patients with treated hypertension or diabetes mellitus: A post hoc analysis of the FMD-J study B
abstract: Abstract We investigated cross-sectional associations between body mass index (BMI) and brachial–ankle pulse wave velocity (baPWV) and longitudinal associations between body weight change and baPWV over 3 years in 874 patients with treated hypertension or diabetes mellitus without coronary artery disease (475 men; mean age, 61.9 ± 9.5 years). baPWV was measured at baseline, 1.5 years, and 3 years. At baseline, BMI was inversely correlated with baPWV ( r = −0.14, P < 0.001), and multivariate analysis confirmed this association (β = −12.5, P < 0.001). In generalized linear mixed-effects models adjusted for concurrent systolic blood pressure, heart rate, and other covariates, neither continuous percentage change in body weight (β = −1.2, P = 0.08) nor categorical body weight change (≥5% increase: β = −10.6, P = 0.45; ≥5% decrease: β = 18.0, P = 0.15) was associated with longitudinal changes in baPWV, with no interaction across baseline BMI categories. The modest body weight changes observed in this cohort were not significantly associated with longitudinal changes in baPWV.

Associations of skin sympathetic nerve activity with orthostatic hypertension and nocturnal hypertension
abstract: Excessive sympathetic activity may contribute to orthostatic hypertension and nocturnal hypertension. However, evidence on associations between skin sympathetic nerve activity (SKNA), assessed noninvasively using neuECG, and these hypertension phenotypes is limited. In this cross-sectional observational study, simultaneous SKNA and supine-to-standing blood pressure (BP) measurements were performed among outpatients with hypertension to examine these associations. Average SKNA (aSKNA) during supine and standing periods, and the percentage change in aSKNA from supine to standing (aSKNA%-change supine-to-standing ) were calculated. Orthostatic hypertension was defined as a supine-to-standing BP increase ≥20/10 mm Hg or conversion from supine-to-standing was correlated with standing SBP (r s = 0.221) and nighttime SBP (r s = 0.280). The adjusted odds ratio (OR) (95% CI) for orthostatic hypertension comparing the highest with the lowest tertile of aSKNA%-change supine-to-standing was 2.18 (0.89-5.35). The corresponding OR for nocturnal hypertension was 2.74 (1.01-7.41) after adjustment for age and sex, and the corresponding OR for nondipping and riser patterns was 3.70 (1.38-9.90). In the current analysis, greater standing-induced increases in aSKNA tended to be associated with orthostatic and nocturnal hypertension, suggesting the potential role of SKNA in characterizing hypertension phenotypes associated with excessive sympathetic activity.

title: Association of winter indoor-temperature variability with 5-year changes in home blood pressure: the Smart Wellness Housing Cohort Survey in Japan
abstract: Abstract Cold indoor temperatures acutely raise blood pressure, but their long-term effects remain uncertain. We investigated whether winter indoor-temperature levels and temporal variability were associated with 5-year changes in home blood pressure. This nationwide cohort included 700 adults from 483 households with complete data. Living-room temperature was measured at 10-min intervals, and home blood pressure was measured twice each morning and evening for 2 weeks in winter at baseline and at the 5-year follow-up. Linear mixed-effects models with household random intercepts were adjusted for baseline blood pressure, individual covariates, and mean indoor temperature in analyses of variability. Mean and minimum indoor temperatures were not associated with 5-year changes in systolic or diastolic home blood pressure. In contrast, a 10 °C/day higher cumulative indoor-temperature variation was associated with 0.42 mmHg (95% confidence interval, 0.04–0.80) and 0.27 mmHg (0.01–0.54) greater increases in systolic and diastolic home blood pressure, respectively. Each additional daily indoor-temperature swing ≥3 °C and ≥5 °C was associated with 0.32 mmHg (0.004–0.636) and 0.49 mmHg (0.04–0.93) greater increases in systolic blood pressure, respectively. A model-based comparison of cumulative indoor-temperature variation values 1 standard deviation above versus below the mean yielded an estimated difference of 1.47 mmHg (0.13–2.81) in the 5-year change in home systolic blood pressure. The sensitivity analysis yielded broadly consistent results. Greater winter indoor-temperature variability was associated with larger 5-year increases in home blood pressure independently of mean indoor temperature. title: Managing hypertension in the aging dragon: bridging the 2026 Taiwan (THS) and 2025 Japanese (JSH) perspectives on blood pressure control in older adults
Key highlights of the 2026 Taiwan Hypertension Society guidelines for the management of hypertension in older adults
authors: the Taiwan Hypertension Society Task Force on Hypertension in Older Adults
abstract: Taiwan, in common with other high-income East Asian societies, is experiencing rapid demographic aging. Hypertension is present in the majority of older adults and remains the leading modifiable determinant of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality in this population. Yet managing blood pressure (BP) in older adults differs qualitatively from managing it in younger patients: arterial stiffening, salt sensitivity, orthostatic BP dysregulation, atrial fibrillation, frailty, cognitive vulnerability, and multimorbidity collectively alter the benefit-harm balance in ways that conventional guidelines-designed predominantly around middle-aged trial populations-do not adequately capture. To address this gap, the Taiwan Hypertension Society (THS) published the 2026 Guidelines for the Management of Hypertension in Older Adults, endorsed by the Taiwan Society of Cardiology (TSOC), the Taiwan Association of Gerontology and Geriatrics (TAGG), and the Taiwan Society of Family Medicine (TSFM). The guideline comprises 63 actionable recommendations developed through PICO-formulated clinical questions, systematic evidence appraisal, and the GRADE approach, with structured expert consensus for areas of limited evidence. Key updates include a measurement-first framework centered on validated oscillometric devices and the 7-2-2 home BP monitoring (HBPM) protocol; age- and comorbidity-stratified systolic BP (SBP) targets with frailty-sensitive safeguards; structured lifestyle prescriptions packaged as the SP-ABCDE mnemonic; individualized pharmacological management with explicit deprescribing considerations; and dedicated sections on orthostatic hypotension, atrial fibrillation, cognitive impairment, and resistant hypertension. This article summarizes the major highlights and clinical implications of the 2026 THS Hypertension guideline for older adults. Key components of the 2026 Taiwan Hypertension Society (THS) Guidelines for the Management of Hypertension in Older Adults. The upper panels summarize the diagnostic and lifestyle foundations-including the 7-2-2 home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) protocol and the SP-ABCDE lifestyle prescription-together with the age- and risk-stratified systolic blood pressure (SBP) targets. For the intensive-versus-standard target comparison, an SBP target of <130 mmHg is a Strong recommendation for general older adults aged 65-79 years but a Conditional recommendation for those aged ≥80 years; a more intensive target of <120 mmHg may be considered (Conditional recommendation) in high-risk older adults with two or more additional cardiovascular risk factors. The lower panels summarize precision targets and frailty safeguards-including individualized targets and deprescribing considerations in frail older adults-and emphasize accurate BP measurement as a patient-safety strategy, including screening for orthostatic hypotension to prevent falls and syncope. Age-specific prognostic value of 1-year changes in cardio-ankle vascular index
abstract: The prognostic significance of longitudinal changes in the cardio-ankle vascular index (CAVI) remains unclear. We investigated the association between 1-year changes in CAVI and subsequent cardiovascular events according to age. A total of 4032 participants with cardiovascular risk factors who were enrolled in the prospective multicenter Coupling Registry and had undergone CAVI measurements at baseline and 1 year were classified into four groups using a CAVI cutoff of 9: good ( < 9 at both time points, n = 1841), improved ( ≥ 9 to <9, n = 268), worsened ( < 9 to ≥9, n = 408), and persistently high ( ≥ 9 at both time points, n = 1515). The primary outcome was a composite of stroke, coronary artery disease, sudden cardiac death, heart failure, and aortic dissection. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models assessed associations between CAVI changes and outcomes. CAVI increased from 8.80 ± 1.34 at baseline to 8.88 ± 1.35 at 1 year ( P < 0.001). During a median 60-month follow-up (49–63 months), 155 cardiovascular events occurred. In the overall cohort, neither the worsened group (HR, 1.56; 95% CI, 0.93–2.62) nor the persistently high group (HR, 1.10; 95% CI, 0.72–1.68) was significantly associated with cardiovascular events compared with the good group. Among participants aged <65 years, the worsened group (HR, 3.36; 95% CI, 1.18–9.58) and persistently high group (HR, 2.68; 95% CI, 1.11–6.50) had higher cardiovascular risk. No significant associations were observed among participants aged ≥65 years. In conclusion, among patients aged <65 years with cardiovascular risk factors, both worsening and persistently elevated CAVI were independently associated with increased cardiovascular risk.

title: Real-world morning home blood pressure in a personal health record application and the risk of cardiovascular events
abstract: Abstract We aimed to assess whether home blood pressure (BP) self-recorded through a personal health record (PHR) application in a real-world setting was associated with cardiovascular disease (CVD) events among individuals not receiving antihypertensive treatment. Using an insurer-based database that links annual health checkup records and home BP self-recorded in the “kencom” PHR application, 6654 participants (mean age: 51.8 ± 9.1 years, males: 68.0%) not receiving antihypertensive treatment were selected. Morning home BP was calculated as the average of morning values over the first 28 days. Office BP was derived from annual health checkup data. The primary outcome was total CVD identified from hospitalization claims. Cox models were used to assess hazard ratios (HRs). The average of home systolic/diastolic BP was 124.5 ± 13.7/80.9 ± 10.9 mmHg, and 80.6% entered their home BP manually. The correlation between home and office BP was r = 0.56 for systolic and r = 0.61 for diastolic BP. During a mean follow-up of 2.79 ± 1.76 years (18,592 person-years), 447 total CVD events occurred. The HRs for total CVD per 1-SD higher in BP were 1.31 for home systolic, 1.12 for office systolic, 1.32 for home diastolic, and 1.21 for office diastolic BP. Results were consistent for stroke and heart failure. When home and office BP were entered simultaneously into the same model, only home systolic/ diastolic BP was independently associated with total CVD risk. Morning home BP self-recorded by users in a PHR application under real-world conditions was more strongly associated with CVD than office BP, supporting the potential value of PHR-based home BP.
